newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left must hold line on euro-Communist party.
newsitem.headline: French left must hold line on euro-Communist party.

text.p: France's Communist party would consider it a breach of its electoral pact with the Socialist party if the left stuck to the timetable for monetary union in the event of winning power in the March 25/June 1 parliamentary election, a party official said on Wednesday.

Francis Wurtz, in charge of the Communist's international department, said he thought it would be impossible for France to meet Maastricht criteria without a new round of austerity, something the Socialist party has pledged not to impose.
If would also be impossible for the Socialists to win backing for conditions it has made for supporting the launch of Economic and Monetary Union in 1999.
"Therefore, if these conditions are not met, that means the march towards the euro can no longer be accepted," he said in an interview.
"(Socialist leader) Lionel Jospin has made a commitment. He must respect it," Wurtz said.

The Socialist party has said it will back the euro only on condition that there be a European economic government, that Italy and Spain join from the start, that there be a growth and solidarity pact and that the euro should not be overvalued against the dollar.
Wurtz repeated a call for a renegotiation of the Maastricht treaty and a new referendum on monetary union.
The Communists and Socialists signed an electoral pact which could allow them to govern together in the event of a left-wing victory, though they do not have a common manifesto.

Their "joint declaration" signed on April 29 includes "a refusal of an ultra-liberal Europe, a refusal to sacrifice the country and its sovereignty to European integration, and a commitment to ask our partners for renegotiations to redirect the building of Europe," he said.
"The very concept of the single currency has the reduction in the cost of labour written in, along with cuts in public spending to favour financial investment," Wurtz said.
"Important decision-making centres, like the European Central Bank, will be independent from governments and totally inaccessible to the people," he added.
The Communist party would favour a delay to the launch of the euro to seek an alternative.

"Everyone in the (centre-right) majority has always been deeply sure that the decision would be a political one and that the nth decimal place could give way to historic and political considerations," Juppe told Les Echos. It released an advance copy of the interview, which will be published on Thursday.

France has insisted countries wishing to join EMU should stick to a Maastricht treaty criterion limiting budget deficits to three percent of Gross Domestic Product this year. But the opposition Socialists, campaigning ahead of a two-round parliamentary election on May 25/June 1 have argued for a flexible interpretation of the treaty.

Juppe said the euro should bring stability and growth. "That implies as President (Jacques Chirac) often says, the participation of as many countries as possible which meet the criteria, including Italy and Spain.

"It also implies an economic policy of the European Union that is oriented towards growth and is not simply determined by the central bank. Obviously exchange rate parities, in particular against the dollar and the yen, must not be artificial but reflect economic reality."
